Barcelona Crime Map:
Safety Index

Crime analysis across Catalunya's 59 police zones: a composite safety index benchmarked against Spain's national average, with trends from 2019 to 2025.

Written byAlexander Semenov
Crime statistics in Catalunya are publicly available — but understanding them takes patience. I built this map to make sense of the data: a composite safety index across 12 crime types, mapped by police zone, with trends since 2019 and a comparison against Spain's national average.

Context

This map vs.
the official map

The Mossos d'Esquadra publish detailed crime statistics through the ICGC crime map viewer — a solid resource covering all 59 ABP police zones across Catalunya, with yearly data going back to 2019. There you can filter by crime type, see charts per zone, and compare against the Catalan average. It's a useful starting point, and I used it constantly while building this.

After spending time with it, though, I kept running into the same gaps. There's no composite safety score — you have to click through each crime type one by one, which makes it hard to get an overall feel for a zone. There's no comparison with Spain, only with Catalunya. And spatial trends are invisible: you can pull a chart for a single zone, but not a regional view of which areas are getting better or worse over time.

Findings

What the data
revealed

01

Barcelona averages 2–4× worse than the Spanish national average

For an average Spanish person relocating to Barcelona, crime rates feel dramatically higher than back home. Across the zones shown — Sant Martí (×2.9), Eixample (×3.6), Gràcia (×1.9) — the pattern is consistent. Catalunya's average is already elevated compared to most Spanish regions, and Barcelona pulls it further.

02

Cornellà de Llobregat is one of the safest zones in the metro area

Safety index vs. Catalonia: 0.775, rank 23 of 59. Cornellà consistently comes out among the safest neighborhoods in the Barcelona metropolitan area — a fact that rarely gets attention because it isn't a central district. The subjective feeling matches the numbers.

03

Sants-Montjuïc ranks 57 out of 59 — which surprised me

Safety index vs. Catalonia: 1.672, rank 57 of 59. That puts Sants-Montjuïc near the bottom of the ranking, yet Sants feels safe day-to-day. The likely explanation is that the ABP zone also includes Montjuïc hill, the port, and industrial areas that pull the average up.

04

Roses has the highest home intrusion rate in Catalunya

The Alt Empordà – Roses zone recorded the highest home intrusion rate in Catalunya in 2025 — 0.087 per 1,000 residents, ×10 the Catalan average. Seasonal vacancy is likely a driver: empty holiday homes are a well-documented target.

05

Home intrusion hasn't declined anywhere in five years

Across all 59 ABP zones, the 2019–2025 trend is flat or rising. Not a single zone shows a sustained downward trend over the full period. This isn't isolated spikes, but a consistent pattern across both urban and rural zones.

06

Assault is rising across the entire region

The trend map shows upward arrows across virtually every zone. This is not a city-specific phenomenon: rural and coastal zones are affected as well.

07

Theft in Barcelona is actually declining

Despite Barcelona's reputation for pickpocketing, theft rates have been falling across most central zones over the last two years. It is a notable counterpoint to the rising assault numbers, although Barcelona's overall indexes remain high.

Methodology

How the index
was built

  1. Open data from Mossos d'Esquadra

    Crime statistics downloaded from the ICGC viewer — 1,520 vector tiles across every ABP zone. Spanish national averages were parsed from the Ministry of Interior annual report.

  2. Composite safety index

    A weighted mean across 12 crime types, normalised against Catalan and Spanish averages. Homicide, assault, sexual crimes, robbery, and theft are weighted higher than drug offences or public disorder.

A note on limitations: Crime weights are subjective and reflect my priorities for outdoor safety. The Spain comparison covers 9 of 12 crime types for 2025. ABP zones are large areas; a high-crime zone can contain safe and unsafe pockets the data cannot distinguish.
